title: Psychological change and mental health enquiry
blurb: Ask the Whooley and GAD-2 questions well, act on the answers, and recognise who needs specialist perinatal mental health care.
question: At her booking appointment, Funmi, 10 weeks, says that over the past month she has often had little interest or pleasure in doing things. She scores 2 on the GAD-2. She has no history of severe mental illness. What should the midwife do next?

teach.h: Emotional change, and when it is more than that
teach.body: Formally: NICE CG192 asks maternity professionals to recognise that depression and anxiety disorders (including GAD, OCD, panic disorder, phobias and PTSD) are under-recognised in pregnancy and the year after birth, and to enquire about mental health as part of routine care. In plain English: pregnancy can be stressful and some worry and changing emotions are expected, but depression or anxiety can start for the first time, or return, now. Asking every woman, kindly and routinely, is how it is found.
teach.cite: NICE CG192 1.5.3–1.5.8; NHS 'Mental health in pregnancy' (2026)

teach.h: Why women may not tell you
teach.body: Women may not disclose because of stigma, fear of being seen as a bad mother, or fear that their baby will be taken into care. Some find it hard to engage because of avoidance or alcohol or drug dependence. Ask as part of a general conversation about wellbeing, be non-judgemental and compassionate, explain that mental health problems are not uncommon and that treatment helps, and be honest about when information is shared.

teach.caption: NICE CG192 1.5.9–1.5.12 and 1.7.3. Women on prescribed medicines should not stop them without advice.

teach.body: Funmi has answered yes to a Whooley question, so her depression screen is positive; her GAD-2 score of 2 is below the threshold. The midwife thanks her for being open, explains that low mood in pregnancy is common and treatable, and either uses the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a fuller assessment or refers her to her GP. She checks there is no history of severe illness, documents the plan and agrees how Funmi can get help between appointments.

teach.text: Do not mix up the tools: Whooley asks about the past MONTH (depression); GAD-2 asks about the last 2 WEEKS (anxiety). A positive screen is not a diagnosis, and sudden psychosis is an emergency (4 hours), not a routine referral (2 weeks).

items: Ask Whooley + GAD-2 at booking and early postnatally; consider them at every contact.
Whooley positive: EPDS or PHQ-9 within a full assessment, or refer to GP.
GAD-2 3 or more: GAD-7 or refer; under 3 with concern: ask about avoidance.
At first contact ask about past or present severe illness, specialist treatment and family history.
Severe illness or history: refer to secondary (ideally specialist perinatal) care.
Postpartum psychosis: be alert in the first 2 weeks; assessment within 4 hours.

summary: You can now ask the Whooley and GAD-2 questions at the right times, interpret the answers and choose the next step. You can also identify women who need specialist perinatal mental health care and the timescales that apply, including the 4-hour standard for suspected postpartum psychosis.

A.q: Which two questions are the depression identification (Whooley) questions recommended by NICE CG192?
options: Feeling nervous or on edge; unable to stop worrying
Thoughts of self-harm; feeling a burden to others
Feeling down or hopeless; little interest or pleasure
Poor sleep; a change in appetite over the past month
A.why: The Whooley questions ask whether, during the past month, she has often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless, or by having little interest or pleasure in doing things (CG192 1.5.4).

whyNot.0: These are the GAD-2 anxiety questions.
whyNot.1: These relate to risk assessment, not the two Whooley questions.
whyNot.3: Sleep and appetite change are common in pregnancy and are not the Whooley questions.

A.q: A woman's GAD-2 score at booking prompts the midwife to consider the GAD-7 or a GP referral. What score triggers this?
options: A score of 3 or more
A score of 2 or more
A score of 4 or more
A score of 5 or more
A.why: CG192 1.5.6: if a woman scores 3 or more on the GAD-2, consider the GAD-7 or referral to her GP (or a mental health professional if severe illness is suspected).

whyNot.1: A score of 2 is below the CG192 threshold.
whyNot.3: Waiting for 5 would miss women with clinically important anxiety.

A.q: According to NICE CG192, when should the Whooley questions and GAD-2 be asked or considered?
options: At booking and again at the 36-week appointment
At the 6 to 8 week postnatal check with her GP
When the woman herself says that she feels low
At booking, early postnatally and at later contacts
A.why: CG192 1.5.4 and 1.5.8: ask at booking and in the early postnatal period, and consider asking at all later contacts in pregnancy and the first year.

whyNot.0: Enquiry is not limited to two antenatal visits.
whyNot.1: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks misses earlier opportunities.
whyNot.2: Routine enquiry is proactive; many women do not raise it themselves.

B.q: At booking, Lucy answers yes to feeling down and hopeless during the past month. There is no suggestion of severe illness. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Refer her urgently to the perinatal mental health crisis team
Use the EPDS or PHQ-9 in a full assessment, or refer to GP
Repeat both sets of questions at her 28-week appointment
Reassure her that some low mood is normal in pregnancy
B.why: A positive Whooley response: consider the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment, or refer to her GP; refer to a mental health professional if severe illness is suspected (CG192 1.5.5).

whyNot.0: Crisis referral is for suspected severe illness or risk, which is not present here.
whyNot.2: Waiting until 28 weeks delays assessment of a positive screen.
whyNot.3: Dismissing a positive screen risks missing depression.

B.q: Hana scores 1 on the GAD-2, but the midwife remains concerned she may have an anxiety disorder. What should the midwife ask next?
options: The two Whooley questions again
Whether she sleeps well at night
Whether she has a family history of anxiety
Whether she avoids places or activities
B.why: CG192 1.5.7: with a GAD-2 score under 3 but continuing concern, ask 'Do you find yourself avoiding places or activities and does this cause you problems?'

whyNot.0: The Whooley questions screen for depression, not anxiety.
whyNot.1: Sleep is often disturbed in pregnancy and is not the CG192 follow-up question.
whyNot.2: Family history is not the next step recommended for this situation.

B.q: At booking, Kate says she was admitted to a psychiatric unit with bipolar disorder 5 years ago and is currently well. What should the midwife do?
options: Refer to secondary, ideally perinatal, mental health care
Ask the Whooley questions at each visit and refer if positive
Ask her GP to review her at the routine postnatal check
Refer to a mental health service if symptoms recur
B.why: CG192 1.5.10: refer all women with any history of severe mental illness to a secondary mental health service (preferably specialist perinatal) and make sure the GP knows.

whyNot.1: Screening alone is not enough for a history of severe illness.
whyNot.2: This delays specialist input until after the highest-risk period.
whyNot.3: Referral is based on her history, before symptoms recur.

C.q: On day 4 after birth, Nadia, who has a history of bipolar disorder, is suddenly confused, has not slept and believes her baby is in danger from the staff. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Refer for an assessment within 2 weeks
Ask the GP to review her within 24 hours
Refer for assessment within 4 hours
Reassure her that this is likely to be baby blues
C.why: Sudden onset of symptoms suggesting postpartum psychosis: refer to a secondary (preferably specialist perinatal) mental health service for immediate assessment, within 4 hours of referral (CG192 1.5.12).

whyNot.0: Two weeks is the standard for routine referrals, not suspected psychosis.
whyNot.1: A GP review within 24 hours is too slow and not the specialist route.
whyNot.3: Confusion, sleeplessness and delusional beliefs are not baby blues.

C.q: During the mental health questions, Rhiannon asks, 'If I tell you how I really feel, will social services take my baby?' Which response is most appropriate?
options: Promise that what she says will stay strictly confidential
Acknowledge her fear and explain that the aim is support
Move on and return to the questions at her next visit
Explain that she has to answer for her baby's safety
C.why: Fear of the baby being taken into care is a recognised barrier (CG192 1.5.1). Responding non-judgementally, explaining that mental health problems are common and treatable and that the aim is support, encourages honest disclosure (1.3.1, 1.4.1).

whyNot.0: Confidentiality cannot be promised absolutely; safeguarding concerns may need to be shared.
whyNot.2: Avoiding the subject loses the opportunity and may reinforce her fear.
whyNot.3: Pressuring her is unlikely to support disclosure and is not compassionate care.

C.q: Ellie is referred to mental health services at 20 weeks with suspected moderate depression. What timescales does NICE CG192 set?
options: Assessment within 4 hours; therapy within 1 week
Assessment within 6 weeks; therapy within 3 months
Assessment within 72 hours; therapy within 2 weeks
Assessment within 2 weeks; therapy within 1 month
C.why: CG192 1.7.3: assess for treatment within 2 weeks of referral and provide psychological interventions within 1 month of initial assessment.

whyNot.0: Four hours is the standard for suspected postpartum psychosis.
whyNot.1: These delays are longer than CG192 allows.
whyNot.2: These are not the CG192 timescales.

reteach.title: Four quick questions, then listen
reteach.question: Think of the enquiry as a doorway: two questions about mood, two about worry, then space to talk. What opens the door, and what happens once it is open?

blocks.body: Mood: the two Whooley questions about the past month. Worry: the two GAD-2 questions about the last 2 weeks, scored 0 to 3 each. History: any past or present severe mental illness, specialist treatment, or severe perinatal illness in her mother or sister. Each answer points to a next step, and a kind, unhurried manner is what makes honest answers possible.

blocks.text: A screen identifies who needs more assessment; it does not diagnose. Do not reassure away a positive answer.

explain.body: During the past month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless? During the past month, have you often been bothered by having little interest or pleasure in doing things? A yes to either is a positive screen.

test.q: What time frame do the Whooley depression questions refer to?
options: During the past month
Over the last 2 weeks
Over the last 6 months
Since she became pregnant
test.why: Both Whooley questions begin 'During the past month...' (CG192 1.5.4).

whyNot.1: Two weeks is the GAD-2 time frame.
whyNot.2: Six months is not the Whooley time frame.
whyNot.3: The questions are anchored to the past month, not the whole pregnancy.

explain.body: Each GAD-2 item is scored: not at all 0, several days 1, more than half the days 2, nearly every day 3. A total of 3 or more prompts the GAD-7 or a GP referral.

test.q: A woman says she has felt nervous and on edge 'nearly every day'. How is this item scored on the GAD-2?
test.why: On the GAD-2, 'nearly every day' scores 3 (CG192 1.5.4).

whyNot.1: 2 is the score for 'more than half the days'.
whyNot.3: 0 is the score for 'not at all'.

explain.body: At first contact ask about past or present severe mental illness, past or present treatment by a specialist mental health service (including inpatient care), and severe perinatal mental illness in a first-degree relative (mother, sister or daughter).

test.q: Which question about family history does NICE CG192 recommend at a woman's first contact in pregnancy?
options: Any mental illness in her grandparents or aunts
Severe perinatal illness in her mother or sister
Depression in any member of her partner's family
Childhood anxiety or ADHD in any of her siblings
test.why: CG192 1.5.9: ask about any severe perinatal mental illness in a first-degree relative (mother, sister or daughter).

whyNot.2: The question concerns the woman's own first-degree relatives.
whyNot.3: The question is about severe perinatal illness, not childhood anxiety.

explain.body: If a woman has past or present severe mental illness, or a family history of severe perinatal illness in a first-degree relative, be alert for symptoms of postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after birth. Sudden symptoms need assessment within 4 hours of referral.

test.q: For a woman with a history of severe mental illness, during which period after birth should the midwife be especially alert for postpartum psychosis?
options: The first 72 hours
The first 6 weeks
The first 12 months
The first 2 weeks
test.why: CG192 1.5.11: be alert for possible symptoms of postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after childbirth.

whyNot.0: 72 hours is too short; psychosis can present later in the first 2 weeks.
whyNot.1: Six weeks is not the CG192 window for heightened alert.
whyNot.2: Twelve months is the overall postnatal period, not the specific alert window.
